slides.title: Bioinformatics: biology as computation
slides.body:
**Bioinformatics**: the science of storing, retrieving, analyzing, and interpreting biological data — overwhelmingly molecular sequence + structure + functional data. Distinct from but overlapping with **computational biology** (modeling biological systems mathematically + computationally) and **systems biology** (integrative network-level biology).

The field emerged from molecular biology's need to manage exploding sequence data — first protein sequences (Margaret Dayhoff's atlas 1965, the first sequence database; PAM matrices 1978), then DNA (GenBank 1982), then whole genomes (Haemophilus influenzae 1995 — Venter + Smith, first complete bacterial genome; Saccharomyces cerevisiae 1996, first eukaryote; C. elegans 1998; Drosophila 2000; Human Genome Project draft 2001 / finished 2003 / T2T (telomere-to-telomere) 2022).

**Major sub-fields**:
- **Sequence analysis**: alignment, motif finding, gene prediction, comparative genomics.
- **Genomics**: assembly, annotation, comparative + population.
- **Transcriptomics**: gene expression (microarrays then RNA-seq; single-cell now standard).
- **Proteomics**: protein identification + quantification (mass spectrometry).
- **Metagenomics**: communities of organisms (Tara Oceans, Human Microbiome Project).
- **Structural bioinformatics**: 3D structures (AlphaFold revolution).
- **Phylogenetics + evolution**: trees, dating, selection.
- **Population genetics**: variation, ancestry, GWAS.
- **Clinical / translational**: variant interpretation, pharmacogenomics, oncology.
- **Synthetic biology + biofoundries**: design + measurement pipelines.

**Why now matters**: NGS (next-generation sequencing) has driven the cost-per-genome curve below Moore's law — from $3B + ~13 years for HGP to <$200 + ~24 hours today. Sequencing is no longer the bottleneck; analysis + interpretation are.

**Major software ecosystems**: BWA + Bowtie + minimap2 (alignment); GATK + DeepVariant (variant calling); STAR + HISAT2 + Salmon + kallisto (transcriptomics); Bioconductor + scverse / scanpy (analysis); IGV (visualization); UCSC + Ensembl + NCBI (data); Nextflow + Snakemake (pipelines); Galaxy (no-code workflows). Cloud-native: Terra, Seven Bridges, DNAnexus.

slides.title: Genome anatomy: from DNA to RNA to protein
slides.body:
**Central dogma**: DNA → (transcription) → RNA → (translation) → protein. With many additional regulatory layers + exceptions (reverse transcription, RNA-directed DNA modification, non-coding RNAs, epigenetic inheritance).

**Human genome at a glance**:
- ~3.1 billion base pairs (haploid).
- ~20000-25000 protein-coding genes.
- ~2% protein-coding sequence.
- ~10% conserved/functional (regulatory + ncRNA).
- ~50% repetitive elements (LINEs, SINEs, LTRs, simple repeats).
- 23 chromosomes (22 autosomes + X + Y).
- ~99.9% identical between any two humans; ~0.1% variation (~3M SNVs + indels + larger).

**Genome structure**:
- **Genes** (transcribed): promoters + 5'UTR + exons + introns + 3'UTR.
- **Regulatory elements**: enhancers, silencers, insulators (3D contacts mediated by CTCF, cohesin).
- **Non-coding RNAs**: rRNA, tRNA, snoRNA, miRNA, lncRNA, circRNA.
- **Transposable elements (TEs)**: Alu, L1, ERVs; some still active.
- **Centromeres + telomeres** (T2T resolved 2022 with long-read assemblies).
- **Heterochromatin**: dense, gene-poor, repetitive; pericentromeric + Y chromosome.
- **Pseudogenes** (~14000 in humans): non-functional gene copies.
- **3D organization**: TADs, A/B compartments, loops (Hi-C, micro-C).

**Variation types**:
- **SNVs (single-nucleotide variants)**: most common; ~3M per individual.
- **Indels**: insertions + deletions (<50 bp).
- **SVs (structural variants)**: large duplications, deletions, inversions, translocations.
- **CNVs**: copy-number variants.
- **Mobile-element insertions**: active L1, Alu, SVA.
- **STRs / VNTRs**: short tandem repeats; forensic + disease.
- **Mosaicism**: post-zygotic variation; tumors.

**Other genomes**:
- Bacterial: 0.5-10 Mb; 90%+ coding.
- Yeast: ~12 Mb.
- Fly: ~140 Mb.
- Mouse: ~2.5 Gb (similar to human).
- Maize: ~2.3 Gb; lots of TE.
- Wheat hexaploid: ~17 Gb.
- Lungfish + onion: >100 Gb (paradox of size).
- Largest: Paris japonica plant ~150 Gb.

**FASTA, GFF, BED, VCF, BAM/CRAM, SAM, FASTQ** — core file formats. Master them.

slides.title: Sequencing technology: short, long, and single-cell
slides.body:
**Sanger sequencing** (1977, Nobel 1980): chain termination; capillary; long-dominant until ~2008. Still gold standard for small validations.

**Next-generation sequencing (NGS)**:
- **Illumina** (~2008+ via Solexa acquisition): sequencing-by-synthesis with reversible terminators; 50-300 bp paired-end reads; ~0.1% error rate; very high throughput. Dominant for most applications. NovaSeq, NextSeq, MiSeq + MiSeq i100, NovaSeqX.
- **Ion Torrent**: H+ detection; cheap; some niche use.
- **454 (Roche)**: pyrosequencing; discontinued.
- **DNBSEQ (MGI/BGI)**: rolling-circle nanoball sequencing; cost-competitive with Illumina.

**Long-read / third-generation**:
- **PacBio (Pacific Biosciences)** HiFi: zero-mode-waveguide single-molecule; 10-25 kb reads, >99% accurate (HiFi CCS). Best for assemblies + structural-variant detection.
- **Oxford Nanopore (ONT)**: protein nanopore detects current changes as DNA threads through; reads up to Mb-scale; ~95% raw accuracy (improving); MinION palm-sized + portable; PromethION high-throughput.

**Single-cell + spatial**:
- **scRNA-seq**: droplet-based (10x Genomics Chromium), well-based (Smart-seq), combinatorial indexing (sci-RNA-seq).
- **scATAC-seq**: chromatin accessibility per cell.
- **Multi-omics**: CITE-seq, SHARE-seq, multiome.
- **Spatial transcriptomics**: Visium, Stereo-seq, MERFISH, seqFISH, Slide-seq.
- **Long-read single-cell**: emerging.

**Cost trajectory**: HGP cost ~$3B + 13 yr (1990-2003); ~$1M / genome in 2008; ~$1000 in 2014; ~$200 in 2024 (Illumina NovaSeqX, MGI). Pace below Moore's law since 2008. Sequencing no longer bottleneck; analysis, sample prep, and ethics are.

**Beyond DNA**:
- Mass spectrometry for proteomics.
- Cryo-EM + X-ray crystallography for structure.
- ATAC-seq, ChIP-seq, Cut&Run for chromatin.
- Hi-C for 3D contacts.
- Whole-organism imaging (light sheet, expansion microscopy).
- Multi-modal integration is the modern frontier.

question.question: Estimate the data scale of a typical whole-genome sequencing experiment
question.goal: Compute approximate file sizes + compute time for human-genome 30× short-read sequencing.

steps.prompt: Total bases sequenced for 30× human genome?

steps.motivation: Each base ~1 byte uncompressed; gzip ~3-4× compression.
steps.reveal: FASTQ contains base + quality score per position + read names. Raw ~180 GB; gzip ~25-30 GB (depending on quality compression). BAM (aligned reads) ~50 GB; CRAM (reference-compressed) ~15-20 GB.

steps.prompt: Alignment time on a modern server (cores × hours)?

acceptedAnswers: a few hours to ~half a day on 16-32 cores

steps.reveal: BWA-MEM throughput ~1-3 Gb/hour/core. 90 Gb on 16 cores → ~2-6 hours. Modern accelerators (DRAGEN, Parabricks) much faster: minutes.

A typical single-sample VCF is ~100 MB-1 GB depending on filters + annotations + indels. gVCF (genomic VCF with all positions) is ~10× larger. Multi-sample joint VCF for population studies scales further.

acceptedAnswers: FASTQ + BAM cold; VCF + analysis warm; cloud-native CRAM increasingly standard

steps.reveal: Modern lifecycle: FASTQ archived (raw evidence); CRAM (reference-compressed BAM) for re-analysis; VCF + annotations for routine work; cloud-native (S3, GCS) with on-demand analysis (Terra, Seven Bridges, DNAnexus). Sequencing a population (e.g., 100k people 30×) needs petabytes.

question.question: Why is bioinformatics often described as 'translating biology into computation'?
options: Modern biology generates data at scales that humans can't manipulate without computers: genomes (gigabases per sample), transcriptomes (millions of reads × thousands of samples), single-cell atlases (billions of cells), proteomes (millions of peptides), connectomes (petabytes of EM data), structures (databases of millions). Bioinformatics provides: (1) data models (FASTA, VCF, GFF, mzML) to represent biological entities; (2) algorithms (alignment, assembly, clustering) to find patterns; (3) statistical frameworks (GWAS, differential expression, multiple testing) for inference; (4) software ecosystems + pipelines for reproducibility. Together they enable comparative + functional biology at genome + atlas scale.
question.explanation: Bioinformatics is the algorithmic + data-engineering layer that makes modern data-rich biology possible. From genome assembly to single-cell atlases to AlphaFold, computational methods are central to biological discovery + clinical translation. The field's tools (data models, algorithms, statistics, software) translate biological questions into computable problems.

hints: What scales modern biology operates at.
slides.workedSolution: Modern biology generates terabytes-petabytes of data per study: genomes, single-cell atlases, proteomes, structures. Bioinformatics provides data models (FASTA, VCF, mzML), algorithms (alignment, assembly, clustering), statistics (GWAS, differential expression), and pipelines (Nextflow, Snakemake) to make this tractable. Without it, comparative + functional biology at scale wouldn't be possible.

question.question: Drag to approximate per-genome sequencing cost in 2024 (USD).
question.explanation: Per-genome cost ~$200-600 in 2024 (Illumina NovaSeqX, MGI competition). Down from $3B for the Human Genome Project (1990-2003). Pace exceeded Moore's law since 2008. Sequencing is no longer the bottleneck for genomics; analysis, sample prep, ethical/regulatory, and clinical interpretation are.

question.question: Match each file format to its content type.
question.explanation: Bioinformatics file ecosystem: FASTQ/FASTA (sequences); SAM/BAM/CRAM (alignments); VCF/BCF (variants); GFF/GTF/BED (features). Each has standards + tooling. Modern pipelines convert raw → aligned → variants → annotations → reports.

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain why the cost-per-genome trajectory drove sequencing from research-only to a routine clinical tool.
question.rubric: Mentions: HGP $3B + 13 yr (1990-2003); $1M per genome 2008; $1000 in 2014; ~$200-600 in 2024. Pace below Moore's law since 2008 due to massively parallel NGS (Illumina, then long-read, then single-cell). Below ~$1000, whole-genome sequencing became viable for clinical settings (rare disease diagnosis, oncology tumor profiling, pharmacogenomics, prenatal testing, infectious disease ID). Specific clinical applications: NICU rapid sequencing (24-48 hr turnaround) for diagnosing rare disorders in neonates; tumor + germline matched pairs for precision oncology; non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT); pathogen ID for sepsis. Now ~3M genomes sequenced (UK Biobank, All of Us, Genomics England, FinnGen). Sequencing no longer the bottleneck; analysis, interpretation, ethical/regulatory, and clinical actionability are. Concludes: cost decline turned genomics from megaproject science into routine medical infrastructure within ~20 years.
